questions.q: What are the three essential environmental conditions required for a seed to begin the process of germination?
questions.a: The three conditions are water, oxygen, and a suitable temperature. A wrong answer (like suggesting "soil" or "fertilizer") indicates the student is confusing germination with later plant growth requirements rather than the specific triggers for the initial start of growth.

questions.q: If you place a dry seed in a sealed, air-tight container with plenty of water and keep it at room temperature, it does not germinate. Why?
questions.a: It lacks oxygen, which is essential for the seed to "breathe" and resume growth. An answer claiming it lacks "soil" reveals a misunderstanding that seeds need nutrients from dirt to *start* germinating, when they actually rely on their own internal stored food first.

questions.q: A student places a seed in a freezer and provides water and air. Will it germinate? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, it will not germinate because the temperature is too low. Germination requires a suitable (warm) temperature to activate the growth process; if the student says "yes because it has water," they are ignoring the temperature trigger.

questions.q: Compare a dormant seed to a germinating seed. What is the most visible physical change the seed undergoes when it absorbs water?
questions.a: The seed swells up and its hard outer coat softens. An answer focusing on the "sprout" alone ignores the crucial first step of moisture absorption that makes the shell pliable enough for the sprout to emerge.

questions.q: Can a seed germinate in the middle of a very hot, dry summer if you only give it oxygen? Justify your decision.
questions.a: No, because it is missing the essential trigger of water, which is required to swell the seed and soften the coat. Answering "yes" ignores the necessity of all three conditions acting together; missing one stops the process.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to prove that water is a necessary trigger for germination.
questions.a: Take two identical sets of dry seeds: keep one set dry and spray the other set with water daily, keeping both in the same room temperature. If only the wet seeds sprout, you have proven water is the trigger. A poor answer fails to keep the temperature and oxygen constant for both groups, making the test unfair.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Seed ______ is the process by which a dormant seed absorbs water, softens its outer coat, and activates its internal stored food to begin growing into a seedling.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever wondered why a dry bean from your kitchen cupboard doesn't grow into a ______, even though it looks perfectly fine?
What is Seed germination? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Seed germination is the process by which a dormant seed absorbs water, softens its outer coat, and activates its internal stored food to begin growing into a seedling.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Seed germination?
questions.a: Students often believe that seeds need soil to germinate.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify the three essential triggers for germination and explain why a seed remains dormant before these conditions are met.
